title: Landmarks
subtitle: Wonders built and natural
about: About a hundred famous landmarks, built and natural, from the Colosseum to Aoraki / Mount Cook. Name the country each one stands in; a few famous border sites need both countries.

cards.note: Built for the 1889 World's Fair, it was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for 41 years, until the Chrysler Building overtook it.
Begun under Emperor Vespasian in AD 72 and finished under Titus in AD 80, it staged gladiator fights, animal hunts and executions.
Built 447 to 438 BC for the goddess Athena; in 1687 a Venetian bomb ignited the Ottoman gunpowder stored inside it.
Its great sarsen circle was raised around 2600 to 2400 BC, aligned with the midsummer sunrise and the midwinter sunset.
Antoni Gaudí took charge in 1883 and devoted the rest of his life to it; at his death in 1926, under a quarter was built.
It began to tilt during construction in the 12th century because of soft ground; work from 1993 to 2001 reduced the lean.
Strictly the nickname of the Great Bell, probably after Sir Benjamin Hall; the tower itself was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012.
Designed chiefly by Bramante, Michelangelo and Maderno, it stands by tradition over the tomb of Saint Peter, beneath its high altar.
Begun in 1869 for King Ludwig II of Bavaria as a romantic retreat honouring Wagner; the king died in 1886, before it was finished.
Built 1555 to 1561 on the orders of Ivan the Terrible to celebrate the capture of Kazan and Astrakhan.
Completed in AD 537 for Emperor Justinian; it became a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1935, and a mosque again in 2020.
Built 1788 to 1791 for King Frederick William II of Prussia; the Berlin Wall blocked the way through it until 1989.
Begun in 1238 by the Nasrid emirs, the last Muslim rulers of al-Andalus; Columbus later won royal backing for his voyage there.
Reachable on foot at low tide, this fortified island remained unconquered throughout the Hundred Years' War.
Begun in 1357 under King Charles IV, it was the only way across the Vltava in the city until 1841.
About 40,000 interlocking basalt columns, mostly hexagonal, left by an ancient volcanic eruption on the County Antrim coast of Northern Ireland.
They run for about 14 kilometres and rise to 214 metres above the Atlantic near O'Brien's Tower, built in 1835.
Edvard Eriksen's small bronze, unveiled in 1913, honours Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale and has been vandalised many times.
Monks built 24 monasteries on top of giant rock pillars from the 14th century; the name means 'lofty', like the word meteor.
The 1,441-room summer residence of the Habsburgs; its name means 'beautiful spring', after an artesian well used by the court.
Built for Expo 58, its nine steel spheres model the unit cell of an iron crystal magnified 165 billion times.
A 16th-century fortress built on a small island in the Tagus, it served explorers as a point of departure and return.
A chain of terraced lakes joined by waterfalls and built up by tufa deposits; it became a national park in 1949.
Listed by UNESCO in 2005 with the Nærøyfjord; its waterfalls include the Seven Sisters and the Suitor, said to be wooing them.
Mined from the 13th century until 1996, it holds underground chapels and statues carved by miners out of rock salt.
Nineteen windmills built around 1740 to drain the surrounding polder, the largest group of old windmills in the country.
A medieval island castle on a lake shore; Lord Byron's 1816 poem The Prisoner of Chillon made its dungeon famous.
Commissioned in 1631 by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as the tomb of his wife Mumtaz Mahal; he is buried there too.
Home to 24 Ming and Qing emperors from 1420 to 1924; legend claims 9,999 rooms, but surveys count 8,886.
Built in the 12th century by King Suryavarman II as a Hindu temple to Vishnu; it later became Buddhist and appears on its nation's flag.
Carved from rose-red sandstone by the Nabataeans; it was unknown to the Western world until Johann Ludwig Burckhardt reached it in 1812.
An active stratovolcano with a famously symmetrical cone; it last erupted in 1707 to 1708 and is a World Heritage cultural site.
Earth's highest mountain above sea level; a joint survey in 2020 measured it at 8,848.86 metres. The border runs over its summit.
Thousands of clay soldiers, horses and chariots buried with the first emperor, Qin Shi Huang; local farmers discovered them in 1974.
Opened in 2010, it took the title of world's tallest building from Taipei 101; it was called Burj Dubai until its inauguration.
The world's largest Buddhist temple, built in the 8th and 9th centuries; its central dome is ringed by 72 Buddhas inside stupas.
The cube-shaped building at the centre of Islam's holiest mosque; Muslims everywhere face it to pray, and pilgrims circle it seven times.
These interlinked 88-storey twin towers were the tallest buildings in the world from 1998 until Taipei 101 overtook them in 2004.
Its name means 'descending dragon'; nearly 2,000 islets, most of them limestone karst towers, rise from its waters.
Begun in 1645 under the 5th Dalai Lama, at about 3,700 metres; it was the Dalai Lamas' residence until 1959.
Sikhism's holiest shrine; Maharaja Ranjit Singh rebuilt it in marble and copper and overlaid the sanctum with gold leaf in 1830.
Capital of the Pagan Kingdom; more than 10,000 Buddhist temples, pagodas and monasteries were built here, and over 2,300 survive.
The top two floors of its Golden Pavilion are coated in gold leaf; a novice monk burned the original down in 1950.
Ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, begun around 515 BC; Alexander the Great's army burned its palaces in 330 BC.
In the 5th century King Kashyapa built his palace on this 180-metre granite rock, reached through a gateway shaped like an enormous lion.
Its name means 'cotton castle'; brilliant white terraces formed by mineral-rich hot springs, with the ancient city of Hierapolis on top.
Built in 1692 around a cave where Padmasambhava, credited with bringing Vajrayana Buddhism to the region, is said to have meditated.
The world's deepest lake, at 1,642 metres, and its oldest; it holds more fresh water than all the North American Great Lakes combined.
The 'Temple of Dawn', named after the Hindu god Aruna; its tall central spire was built in the early 19th century.
Founded in 1395 as the Joseon dynasty's first royal palace; King Sejong led the creation of the Hangul alphabet here.
The heart of Samarkand under the Timurids, framed by three great madrasas with turquoise domes and intricate mosaic tilework.
At least 1,260 grassy mounds on Bohol island whose green cover turns chocolate brown in the dry season, hence the name.
Built around 2500 BC as one of the largest cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation; its name means 'Mound of the Dead Men'.
Tomb of the pharaoh Khufu; the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and the only one still largely intact.
Known locally as Mosi-oa-Tunya, 'the smoke that thunders'; David Livingstone named it after Queen Victoria in 1855.
Africa's highest mountain and the world's highest free-standing one, at 5,895 metres; Hans Meyer first reached its summit in 1889.
Its slopes hold some 2,285 plant species, about four fifths of them fynbos, an Afrikaans word meaning 'fine bush'.
Carved for Ramesses II in the 13th century BC; in the 1960s the twin temples were moved uphill, away from rising Lake Nasser.
Nelson Mandela spent 18 of his 27 years in prison here; the name comes from the old Dutch word for seals.
The largest adobe brick building in the world; the present mosque dates from 1907, on a site used since the 13th century.
Monolithic churches carved down into solid rock, traditionally credited to King Lalibela around 1200 and laid out as a symbolic Jerusalem.
Named after the Maasai people; 'Mara' means 'spotted' in the Maa language, after the bushy trees dotting its plains.
Founded, legend says, by Queen Dido of Tyre; Rome destroyed it in 146 BC at the end of the Third Punic War.
A river delta that never reaches the sea: its floodwaters spread into the Kalahari and almost all evaporate. It was UNESCO's 1,000th World Heritage Site.
A clay pan ringed by towering red dunes; its name roughly means 'dead-end marsh', because the river feeding it has no outlet.
A dirt road lined with giant Grandidier's baobabs, the largest of six baobab species found only on this island.
A fortified clay village on the old caravan route between the Sahara and Marrakesh; its use as a Hollywood film set helped fund its restoration.
Birthplace of Emperor Septimius Severus, who enriched it; long buried under sand dunes, it is one of the best-preserved Roman sites in the Mediterranean.
Royal tombs of the Kingdom of Kush, built from about 270 BC; the last, around AD 350, was Africa's last pyramid.
Its main crater, about two kilometres wide, usually holds a lava lake, at times the most voluminous known in recent history.
A small island off the capital, now a memorial to the Atlantic slave trade; in 1978 it was among UNESCO's first twelve World Heritage Sites.
A gift from the people of France, designed by Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, with a metal framework by Gustave Eiffel; it was dedicated in 1886.
Built around 1450, probably as an estate for the Inca emperor Pachacuti; Hiram Bingham brought it to world attention in 1911.
Carved by the Colorado River, it is more than 1,800 metres deep and exposes nearly two billion years of the planet's geological history.
Built from 1922 to 1931 of reinforced concrete and soapstone atop Corcovado mountain; Romanian sculptor Gheorghe Leonida carved the face.
One of the largest Maya cities, a major centre of the northern Maya lowlands from about AD 600 to 1200.
The world's largest waterfall system; its name comes from Guarani or Tupi words for 'big water'. Most falls are on the Argentine side.
Three falls on the river draining Lake Erie into Lake Ontario; Horseshoe Falls, straddling the border, is North America's most powerful waterfall.
Opened in 1937 with Joseph Strauss as chief engineer, it was then the longest and tallest suspension bridge in the world.
Carved by the Rapa Nui people of Easter Island between 1250 and 1500; every one had been toppled by the late 19th century.
Home to the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon; at its height it was the largest city in the Americas, centuries before the Aztecs.
Charles Darwin studied their many endemic species in the 1830s, and they inspired his theory of evolution by natural selection.
The world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall, named after American aviator Jimmie Angel, the first person to fly over it, in 1933.
The world's largest salt flat; after rain a thin film of water turns it into a vast mirror, and its brine is rich in lithium.
Built by the Canadian National railway and completed in 1976, it was the world's tallest free-standing structure for 32 years.
Made between 500 BC and AD 500 by removing reddish pebbles to expose paler ground; many shapes are best seen from the air.
A Maya city in the rainforest that peaked around AD 200 to 900; one of its ruling dynasties was founded by conquerors from Teotihuacan.
At nearly 7,000 metres, the highest mountain outside Asia and one of the Seven Summits; its normal route needs no technical climbing.
A circular sinkhole 318 metres across and 124 metres deep, formed as a dry cave when sea levels were much lower, then flooded.
Commissioned by revolutionary leader Henri Christophe and built by tens of thousands of former slaves to repel a French invasion that never came.
A neo-Gothic basilica built from 1916 to 1949 in a river canyon; pilgrims believe the image of Mary on its rock wall formed miraculously.
Designed by Danish architect Jørn Utzon, who resigned before it was finished; Queen Elizabeth II opened it in 1973.
Sacred to the Pitjantjatjara, an Aṉangu people; Europeans named it Ayers Rock, and it is now officially gazetted as Uluru / Ayers Rock.
The world's largest coral reef system, over 2,900 reefs stretching more than 2,300 kilometres; it is the biggest structure built by living organisms.
Rudyard Kipling called it the eighth Wonder of the World; the sealer John Grono named it in 1823 after Milford Haven in Wales.
The country's highest mountain, 3,724 metres as of 2014; a rock and ice avalanche in December 1991 knocked ten metres off its summit.
Limestone stacks beside the Great Ocean Road; despite the name there may never have been twelve, and seven still stand.
Its ceilings glitter with Arachnocampa luminosa, a glowworm species found only in this country; visitors drift beneath them by boat.
The country's oldest national park, founded on sacred peaks gifted in 1887 by Te Heuheu Tūkino IV, leading chief of Ngāti Tūwharetoa.
Capital of the Saudeleur dynasty until about 1628, built as 92 artificial islets of stone and coral linked by tidal canals.
It has erupted almost continuously for centuries; its glow is thought to have drawn Captain James Cook to Tanna Island in 1774.
